Enhancing high-solid anaerobic digestion of cattle manure using air 
nanobubble water: Performance improvements and microbial mechanisms 
under thermophilic and mesophilic conditions

A B S T R A C T
High-solid anaerobic digestion (HSAD) is a promising strategy for cattle manure (CM) valorization, but its ef­
ficiency is often limited by slow hydrolysis, acid accumulation, and ammonia inhibition. This study investigated 
the effects of air nanobubble water (Air-NBW) on HSAD of CM under thermophilic (55 ± 1 ◦C) and mesophilic 
(37 ± 1 ◦C) conditions. Batch digesters were operated at CM-to-liquid mass ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4, with 
distilled water as the control. Air-NBW promoted soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) release and volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs) formation, indicating enhanced hydrolysis and acidogenesis. Under thermophilic conditions, 
Air-NBW accelerated both soluble organic matter production and subsequent VFAs conversion, whereas under 
mesophilic conditions it mainly facilitated later-stage VFAs turnover after transient acid accumulation. 
Compared with the corresponding controls, cumulative methane yield increased by 23.1%, 10.2%, and 31.9% at 
thermophilic CM-to-liquid ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4, respectively, and by 21.4%, 15.7%, and 17.4% under 
mesophilic conditions. The modified Gompertz model further indicated improved methane production kinetics. 
Microbial analysis showed that Air-NBW was associated with the enrichment of hydrolytic bacteria and 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens, supporting the coordinated conversion of particulate organics to methane. 
Correlation analysis linked Corynebacterium with SCOD and Methanosphaera with methane production under 
thermophilic conditions, while mesophilic enhancement was more related to VFAs turnover and methanogenic 
recovery. These findings demonstrate that Air-NBW can improve HSAD performance and provide a practical 
strategy for enhancing renewable energy recovery from CM.
1. Introduction
The global intensification of livestock production has led to vast 
accumulations of manure, among which cattle manure (CM) pre­
dominates [1]. Improper handling and disposal of CM can cause air 
emissions, groundwater pollution, soil degradation, and the propagation 
of pathogenic microorganisms [2]. At present, direct land application 
remains the predominant CM management practice [3]; however, CM 
often harbors low levels of heavy metals—which, upon repeated soil 
application, can accumulate (e.g., Cd, Hg), and ultimately threaten crop 
safety [4]. Consequently, devising strategies for CM volume reduction, 
detoxification, and resource recovery has emerged as an urgent priority. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) represents a leading manure-treatment tech­
nology that concurrently reduces waste, detoxifies contaminants, facil­
itates nutrient recovery, and produces renewable biogas [5]. Operating 
temperature and total solids (TS) content critically influence AD per­
formance [6]. Mesophilic AD (25–40 ◦C) is widely implemented due to 
its operational stability [7], whereas thermophilic AD (> 45 ◦C), despite 
its higher energy demands and potential stability issues, offers faster 
hydrolysis rates, increased biogas yields, and enhanced methane

productivity [8]. Therefore, comparative evaluation of AD performance 
under mesophilic versus thermophilic conditions is essential. Total 
solids content affects reactor rheology, organic substrate hydrolysis, and 
inhibitor buildup, thereby exerting a pronounced impact on AD effi­
ciency and biogas yields [9]. Conventional low-TS AD systems (4–7% 
TS) produce large volumes of liquid digestate, which raises handling 
costs and undermines environmental gains [4,10].
High-solid anaerobic digestion (HSAD), defined by TS contents 
above 8%, has emerged as a promising approach for livestock manure 
valorization, offering a compact footprint, high energy conversion effi­
ciency, reduced digestate volumes, and elevated organic loading rates 
[11]. Nevertheless, HSAD is challenged by inherently slow hydrolysis 
kinetics, compromised reactor stability, and suboptimal methanogenic 
activity [12]. For example, the high lignocellulosic content of CM im­
pedes enzymatic hydrolysis, causing reactor inhibition, extended lag 
phases, and stability deterioration, which together diminish methane 
yields and production rates [13]. Moreover, substrates with elevated TS 
levels (e.g., 25% TS agricultural residues) promote the accumulation of 
inhibitory intermediates, such as volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and total 
ammonia nitrogen (TAN), thus suppressing methane production [14]. 
Likewise, when digesting chicken manure at 9% TS, biogas productivity 
decreases from 0.32 to 0.13 L⋅g−1 VS as TAN concentrations rise from 
3000 to 6000 mg⋅L−1 [15]. Accordingly, to enhance economic feasibility 
and operational robustness, it is imperative to integrate innovative 
strategies into HSAD, thereby enabling efficient CM valorization while 
mitigating environmental risks.
Nanobubble water (NBW) technology involves water saturated with 
nanobubbles [16], typically containing 106–108 bubbles per milliliter 
with diameters <1000 nm [17]. It exhibits unique properties distinct 
from ordinary water, such as high specific surface area, enhanced mass 
transfer efficiency, extended stability, elevated water molecule mobility, 
strong diffusivity, and free radical generation capability [18]. Conse­
quently, this technology has found wide applications in fields like ma­
rine environmental restoration, water disinfection, and membrane 
fouling mitigation [19]. In recent years, NBW application in AD has 
gained traction due to the fundamental role of water in AD systems. 
Water not only accelerates substrate hydrolysis but also transports hy­
drolytic products and intermediates to microbial reaction sites [20], 
establishing the feasibility of NBW-AD coupling. Existing studies 
confirm that NBW generated with different gases enhances AD perfor­
mance. For instance, in pig manure AD, NBW addition increased cu­
mulative methane yield (CMY) to 192–225 mL⋅g−1 VSadded, representing 
a 19–39% improvement over the control group [21]. In waste activated 
sludge AD, N2-NBW increased system Zeta potential by 17.1%. Higher 
Zeta potential enhances repulsive forces between sludge particles, 
dispersing flocs to improve microbial-substrate contact and substrate 
accessibility, ultimately boosting methane yield by 29.1% [22]. In food 
waste AD, N2-NBW and Air-NBW increased hydrolysis-related enzyme 
activity by 8–47% in the first stage and methanogenesis-related coen­
zyme activity by 34%, benefiting both hydrolysis and methanogenesis 
phases [23]. Among these, Air-NBW is particularly suitable for practical 
engineering due to its simple preparation, low cost, and environmental 
benignity. However, research on Air-NBW-enhanced AD performance 
remains limited, particularly regarding mechanisms under high-solid 
conditions. This knowledge gap stems partly from the misconception 
that “air is incompatible with AD”. In reality, controlled air introduction 
does not abort AD. On one hand, trace oxygen is rapidly consumed by 
aerobic/facultative bacteria, restoring anaerobic conditions promptly 
[24]. On the other hand, certain methanogens display oxygen tolerance. 
For example, Methanosarcina, Methanocorpusculum, and Methano­
brevibacter can adapt to microaerophilic conditions by synthesizing 
antioxidant enzymes (e.g., superoxide dismutase, catalase, peroxidase) 
and adjusting their community structures in response to oxygen levels 
[25].
Given the technical challenges in HSAD for CM treatment, including 
low hydrolysis efficiency and poor system stability, combined with Air- 
NBW's proven potential to enhance AD performance and the unresolved 
knowledge gap in its mechanistic basis, this study aims to systematically 
evaluate the impact of Air-NBW on CM HSAD performance and disen­
tangle its mechanisms in regulating hydrolysis kinetics, methane pro­
duction, system stability, and microbial community dynamics. The study 
seeks to provide theoretical insights and technical guidance for opti­
mizing CM HSAD, enhancing energy recovery efficiency, and maxi­
mizing environmental benefits.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Fresh CM was collected from the Gansu Holstein Dairy Cattle 
Breeding Demonstration Center and stored at 4 ± 1 ◦C before the 
experiment. The anaerobic digested sludge used as inoculum was 
sourced from Gansu Yanchangbu Sewage Treatment Plant. Following 
collection, the sludge was acclimated under thermophilic (55 ± 1 ◦C) 
and mesophilic (37 ± 1 ◦C) conditions to serve as inoculum. Table 1
presents the key characteristics of thermophilic and mesophilic inocula, 
as well as CM, based on triplicate measurements.
2.2. Air-NBW
Air-NBW was prepared using a nanobubble generator (JWNP, 
AL01S, China). Air gas was introduced into the generator at a controlled 
pressure of 0.4 MPa to 0.5 MPa at a temperature of 20 ± 2 ◦C. DW was 
drawn into the generator's circulation system and cycled for 25 min to 
produce Air-NBW for use throughout the HSAD process in this study. 
The freshly prepared liquid appeared as white opaque micro- 
nanobubble water, which turned into a colorless transparent NBW 
after standing for 5 to 10 min.
2.3. Experimental setup
In this study, batch experiments were conducted using 1 L anaerobic 
fermenters. The sealed lid of the reactor was equipped with two sam­
pling ports with an inner diameter of 6 mm. One port was connected to a 
gas collection bag via a silicone tube (inner diameter 6 mm) for biogas 
collection, while the other port enabled dynamic sampling of digestate 
samples through a peristaltic pump. The substrate used in the experi­
ment was CM, and the inoculum was anaerobic digested sludge accli­
mated at the corresponding temperature (55 ± 1 ◦C/37 ± 1 ◦C). The 
total mass of substrate in each reactor was controlled at 800 g, with 80 g 
of inoculum sludge added. The experimental group used Air-NBW as the 
liquid medium, while the control group used distilled water (DW) as the 
liquid medium. Six operating conditions were established by adjusting 
the mass ratio of CM-to-liquid medium, i.e., 1:1 (TS = 19.4%), 1:2 (TS =
13.1%), and 1:4 (TS = 8.1%). Based on the combination of temperature 
variables (55 ± 1 ◦C/37 ± 1 ◦C) and medium types (Air-NBW/DW), 
each operating condition was systematically named. Under thermophilic 
conditions, the control groups with ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4 were

To simulate actual engineering operating conditions, no artificial pH 
adjustment was performed during the experiment. The reactors were 
placed in constant-temperature water baths at 55 ± 1 ◦C and 37 ± 1 ◦C 
to maintain the reaction temperature, respectively. The reactors were 
manually shaken for 1 min at a fixed time daily to ensure sufficient 
contact between the inoculum and substrate.
2.4. Chemical analyses
Standard methods [26] were used to determine the TS, VS, total 
alkalinity (TA), pH, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), and TAN 
of the digestate samples. The free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was calcu­
lated using a specific formula [27]. The concentration of VFAs was 
determined using a gas chromatograph (SP-7890 Plus, Ruihong, China) 
equipped with a high-performance organic acid column that is 30 m 
long, has an internal diameter of 320 μm, and a film thickness of 0.50 
μm. This system is combined with a flame ionization detector, which 
efficiently separates and quantifies the VFAs by utilizing the differing 
interactions between the acids and the stationary phase of the column. 
The acids are then ionized in the flame to produce measurable signals, 
allowing for the detection of various VFAs. The volume and composition 
of biogas were determined using a gas flow meter (LML-2, Alpha, China) 
and a biogas analyzer (GA 5000, Geotach, United Kingdom), 
respectively.
2.5. Microbial community analysis
Digestate samples for microbial community analysis were collected 
at the early and final stages of AD, corresponding to day 3 and day 60, 
respectively. Before sampling, each reactor was thoroughly mixed to 
ensure sample representativeness. Samples were collected under aseptic 
conditions from triplicate reactors for each treatment and immediately 
stored at −80 ◦C before DNA extraction. The V3-V4 regions of bacterial 
DNA were amplified using primers 341F (CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG) 
and 806R (GGACTACHVGGGTATCTAAT), while the V4-V5 regions of

TAN, FAN, CMY, and methane production rate.
2.6. Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software version 27.0 
for Windows. Significant differences in performance indicators were 
assessed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by 
Tukey's post hoc test. Methane yield data were fitted using a modified 
Gompertz model [28]. The relationships between environmental factors 
and microbial communities were analyzed using Pearson correlation 
analysis. Dominant microbial genera were selected for correlation 
analysis based on their relative abundance (RA) and ecological rele­
vance. Before analysis, microbial RA data were transformed when 
necessary, and environmental variables were standardized to reduce the 
influence of different units and scales. Correlations with P < 0.05 were 
considered statistically significant, and those with P < 0.01 were 
considered highly significant. In the correlation networks, * and ** 
indicate P < 0.05 and P < 0.01, respectively.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Digestion performance
3.1.1. pH
As a critical indicator of the HSAD process, pH exhibited similar 
dynamic trends in both thermophilic (Fig. 1a) and mesophilic (Fig. 1b) 
systems. All reactors experienced a pH drop to minimum values on day 
3: in thermophilic groups, pH decreased from initial 7.7–8.2 to 7.2–7.6, 
whereas in mesophilic groups, it declined from 7.5 to 8.1 to 6.6–6.8. This 
was attributed to the rapid accumulation of VFAs during the hydrolysis 
and acidification phase. However, the extent of pH decrease differed 
markedly between the two temperature regimes. The smaller pH decline 
in the thermophilic reactors suggests that acidification was more effec­
tively buffered under thermophilic conditions. This may be attributed to 
the faster release of ammonia nitrogen from protein degradation and the 
higher alkalinity generated during thermophilic digestion, which partly 
neutralized the acids produced during the early-stage [29,30]. In 
contrast, the sharper pH drop in the mesophilic reactors indicates that 
VFAs production exceeded their consumption by methanogens during 
the initial phase, leading to more evident transient acid stress. This 
interpretation is consistent with the subsequent VFAs and TVFAs/TA 
results.
As the reaction advanced, reactor pH rebounded and stabilized, 
driven by VFAs conversion and utilization alongside gradual increases in 
TAN concentration. Ultimately, thermophilic group pH stabilized at 
8.1–8.2, while mesophilic group pH reached 7.5–7.8. The higher stabi­
lized pH under thermophilic conditions favored acid-buffering capacity, 
but it also implies that FAN-related inhibition should be considered 
together with TAN and temperature, rather than judging stability from 
pH alone. Overall, the pH profiles suggest that Air-NBW-enhanced HSAD 
involved early acidification followed by recovery through VFAs con­
version and alkalinity buffering. After stabilization, pH values in all 
reactors remained within the suitable range for methanogenic meta­
bolism [31].
3.1.2. SCOD
As a primary indicator of the hydrolysis-acidogenesis stage in HSAD, 
SCOD reflects the extent of substrate disintegration and soluble organic 
matter release [32]. Fig. 2 shows that SCOD concentrations in all re­
actors increased initially and then declined. This behavior results from 
SCOD accumulation during hydrolysis and acidogenesis, followed by 
consumption by methanogens converting soluble organics into methane 
and carbon dioxide [33]. Under thermophilic conditions (Fig. 2a), SCOD 
peaked on day 3, reaching 10,724.3–32,922.7 mg⋅L−1, whereas meso­
philic reactors (Fig. 2b) peaked later on day 8 at lower levels 
(5437.8–28,536.0 mg⋅L−1). The earlier SCOD peak under thermophilic 
conditions indicates that elevated temperature accelerated the solubi­
lization of particulate organic matter from CM, while the subsequent 
rapid decline suggests faster conversion of soluble intermediates. In 
contrast, the delayed peak and slower decrease under mesophilic con­
ditions indicate slower hydrolysis and downstream conversion at 37 ◦C, 
consistent with the stronger early pH decline and subsequent VFAs 
accumulation.
The effect of Air-NBW on SCOD depended on both temperature and 
solid-to-liquid ratio. Under thermophilic conditions, Air-NBW increased 
SCOD peaks in the 1:2 and 1:4 groups, especially in T6, where the peak 
was 54.0% higher than that in T5. However, T2 did not exceed T1 in the 
1:1 groups, suggesting that excessive solid loading may mask the pro­
moting effect of Air-NBW because SCOD accumulation is jointly

controlled by substrate solubilization and soluble-organic conversion. 
Under mesophilic conditions, Air-NBW generally increased SCOD peaks, 
with M6 showing a 40.7% higher peak than M5, indicating enhanced 
soluble organic release. Nevertheless, the slower SCOD decline after the 
peak suggests that soluble intermediates were not rapidly converted at 
37 ◦C. Overall, Air-NBW promoted SCOD release, but its effect was 
regulated by temperature and solid loading. Therefore, the enhanced 
methane production in Air-NBW reactors should be attributed not only 
to improved hydrolysis, but also to the subsequent conversion efficiency 
of soluble intermediates during methanogenesis.
3.1.3. VFAs concentration and components
VFAs are key intermediates linking hydrolysis-acidogenesis and 
methanogenesis in HSAD. They mainly consist of short-chain fatty acids, 
including acetic, propionic, and butyric acids [34]. Under thermophilic 
conditions, the VFAs concentrations in all groups reached their peaks on 
day 3 (Fig. 3). Among them, acetic acid is an important substrate for 
methanogenesis and is closely related to methanogenic conversion ef­
ficiency [35]. Air-NBW groups (T2, T4) exhibited acetic acid concen­
trations of 6132.7 and 3400.8 mg⋅L−1, representing 46.3% and 66.1% 
increases over DW controls (T1, T3: 4193.2 and 2047.2 mg⋅L−1), 
respectively. This suggests that Air-NBW promoted the formation of 
readily methanogenic intermediates under thermophilic conditions. 
After the peak, VFAs in thermophilic reactors decreased rapidly, and 
acetate was consumed earlier than propionate and butyrate. This pattern 
indicates that thermophilic digestion supported efficient acid conver­
sion, shortened the period of acid accumulation, and improved meth­
anogenic efficiency. Although T6 showed lower VFAs accumulation than 
some higher-solid groups, its methane performance was higher than that 
of T5, suggesting that Air-NBW may have improved not only interme­
diate production but also the subsequent utilization of VFAs under low- 
solid thermophilic conditions.
Under mesophilic conditions, high-solid loading groups (1:1, 1:2) 
(M1, M2, M3, M4) exhibited continuous VFAs accumulation for the first 
15 days, reaching 15,056.4, 12985.2, 8378.7, and 9363.9 mg⋅L−1, 
respectively, with minimal consumption. This indicates that, at 37 ◦C, 
hydrolysis and acidogenesis proceeded faster than methanogenic con­
sumption during the early-stage, resulting in transient acid accumula­
tion. This interpretation is consistent with the sharper pH decline and 
the later TVFAs/TA results. After day 15, the HSAD system gradually 
recovered, with rapid acetic acid consumption and gradual metabolism 
of propionic/butyric acid to methane within two weeks. Notably, Air- 
NBW groups (M2, M4) exhibited higher conversion efficiency, aligning 
with increased methane yields (see Section 3.1.6), confirming Air-NBW 
enhances VFAs consumption and methanogenic conversion, acceler­
ating system stability recovery.
Overall, thermophilic digestion showed rapid VFAs production fol­
lowed by rapid consumption, reflecting a better coupling between 
acidogenesis and methanogenesis. In contrast, mesophilic digestion 
showed delayed VFAs conversion and a longer acid stress period. Air-

3.1.4. TA and VFAs/TA

from ammonia released during deamination of nitrogenous substrates 
[36]. Under both thermophilic and mesophilic regimes, TA in all di­
gesters rose initially and then reached a plateau (Fig. 4a, b). This in­
crease is attributable to the release of alkali metals (e.g., Ca2+, Mg2+)

from CM, which contribute to TA during digestion [37]. Moreover, TA 
levels scaled with substrate solids content, since higher solid loadings 
correspond to increased nitrogenous organic matter and thus greater 
ammonia release through deamination. However, TA alone cannot fully 
represent process stability. Therefore, the TVFAs/TA ratio was further 
used to evaluate the balance between acid production and buffering 
capacity [38]. TVFAs/TA values below 0.35 denote adequate buffering 
and stable operation, whereas values above 0.8 indicate insufficient 
buffering capacity and potential process instability [4,39]. Under ther­
mophilic conditions, TVFAs/TA reached a maximum on day 3 (Fig. 4c). 
Air-NBW treatments (T2, T4) exhibited TVFAs/TA ratios exceeding 0.8, 
indicating a transient destabilization due to enhanced hydrolysis. This 
transient instability resulted from accelerated VFAs accumulation 
driven by Air-NBW-enhanced hydrolysis. Thereafter, rapid VFAs con­
sumption by methanogens drove TVFAs/TA below 0.35 by day 15, 
stabilizing the system in line with observed VFAs depletion (see Section 
3.1.3). In mesophilic reactors, TVFAs/TA dynamics were delayed and 
fluctuated markedly during the initial 15 days (Fig. 4d). TVFAs/TA 
values in M1–M4 ranged from 0.6 to 1.1 well above the 0.35 threshold 
indicating acid inhibition and instability from VFAs accumulation dur­
ing the first 15 days. As digestion continued, TVFAs/TA gradually 
declined below 0.35 by day 25, reflecting system recovery consistent 
with VFAs depletion trends.
Overall, TA results indicate that CM degradation provided buffering 
capacity, especially at higher solid loadings, whereas TVFAs/TA 
revealed whether this buffering capacity was sufficient to counteract 
acid accumulation. Thermophilic digestion showed a stronger ability to 
recover from early acid stress, while mesophilic digestion experienced a 
longer unstable period due to slower VFAs conversion. Air-NBW 
increased early acidification pressure by promoting hydrolysis, but it 
did not cause persistent instability; instead, its positive effect depended 
on whether VFAs conversion could subsequently keep pace with acid 
production.
3.1.5. TAN and FAN
TAN, a by product of protein hydrolysis, reflects digester hydrolysis 
capacity [40]. Moderate TAN concentrations support microbial growth 
by providing buffering capacity and nutrients. However, TAN concen­
trations >1500 mg⋅L−1 inhibit methanogen activity, reducing methane 
production [41]. In both thermophilic (Fig. 5a) and mesophilic (Fig. 5b) 
systems, TAN concentrations in high-solid (1:1) groups (T1, T2) stabi­
lized at 1985.3–2014.5 mg⋅L−1, while M1 and M2 reached 
1734.5–1960.0 mg⋅L−1, all exceeding 1500 mg⋅L−1 and indicating 
ammonia inhibition risk. In 1:2 and 1:4 ratio groups, TAN stabilized at 
848.2–1482.2 mg⋅L−1 (T3, T4, T5, T6) and 799.0–1260.0 mg⋅L−1 (M3, 
M4, M5, M6), both below the inhibition threshold. Thus, the 1:2 and 1:4 
digesters had a lower risk of TAN-related inhibition. Thermophilic 
groups exhibited higher TAN concentrations, likely due to enhanced 
hydrolytic activity in thermophilic microbial communities, highlighting 
hydrolysis limitations under mesophilic conditions [42].
FAN, a fraction of TAN, is more toxic to methanogens than TAN 
because it can penetrate microbial cell membranes and accumulate 
intracellularly, causing proton imbalance or inactivation of cytoplasmic 
enzymes [43]. When FAN concentration exceeds 250 mg⋅L−1, it will 
inhibit methanogens in HSAD systems [44]. In both thermophilic 
(Fig. 5c) and mesophilic (Fig. 5d) groups, FAN concentrations increased 
rapidly after day 3, and FAN concentrations in thermophilic groups were 
generally higher than those in mesophilic groups, which is due to the 
positive correlation between FAN concentration and pH as well as 
temperature [45]. Among them, the FAN concentrations of thermophilic 
groups T1 and T2 finally stabilized at 289.4–320.3 mg⋅L−1, exceeding 
250 mg⋅L−1, indicating that ammonia inhibition may have occurred in 
digesters with 1:1 ratio under thermophilic conditions. Notably, T2 
exhibited lower FAN concentrations than T1, suggesting that Air-NBW 
may have partially reduced FAN-related stress under thermophilic 1:1 
conditions. Remaining thermophilic groups had stable FAN concentra­
tions of 134.9–210.1 mg⋅L−1, while mesophilic groups showed 
32.7–131.8 mg⋅L−1, all below the inhibition threshold and indicating no 
significant ammonia stress.

substrate loads and thus had the greatest theoretical methane potential, 
their CMY fell below those of T3 and T4 due to ammonia inhibition at 
excessive solids concentrations, as evidenced by TAN and FAN levels 
exceeding inhibitory thresholds (see Section 3.1.5). In T2, Air-NBW 
reduced FAN relative to T1, partially relieving ammonia toxicity and 
thereby contributing to the 23.1% CMY increase. Moreover, T2 achieved 
a specific methane production rate of 24.2 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 versus 
16.4 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 in T1, indicating enhanced conversion effi­
ciency (Fig. 6b). T3 and T4 recorded the highest absolute CMY values, 
yet the relative CMY enhancement in T4 was only 10.2%, and its specific 
methane rate of 19.8 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 only marginally exceeded T3's 
19.1 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1. T5 and T6, with the lowest solids content and 
substrate load, exhibited the lowest CMY values; however, T6 displayed 
the greatest relative CMY increase (31.9%) upon Air-NBW addition and 
achieved a superior specific methane rate of 26.6 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 
versus 19.2 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 in T5.
Under mesophilic conditions, the CMY values for M1–M6 were 
126.0, 153.0, 119.1, 137.8, 56.1, and 65.9 mL⋅g−1 VSadded, respectively 
(Fig. 6c). Air-NBW treatments (M2, M4, M6) enhanced CMY by 21.4%, 
15.7%, and 17.4% compared to their DW controls (M1, M3, M5), 
respectively. Although M1 had the highest TS and substrate load and 
thus the greatest theoretical methane potential, its actual CMY was 
lower than that of M4, likely due to acid inhibition from excessive VFAs 
accumulation. In contrast, M2, which shared the same solids content as 
M1 but was supplemented with Air-NBW, achieved a 21.4% CMY in­
crease, and its specific methane production rate reached 8.3 mL⋅g−1 
VSadded d−1 versus 6.7 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 in M1 (Fig. 6d), suggesting 
that Air-NBW may have facilitated recovery from acid inhibition. M4 
recorded the highest absolute CMY; however, its relative enhancement 
versus M3 was modest (15.7%), and its specific methane rate (8.2 
mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1) only marginally exceeded M3's 7.6 mL⋅g−1 VSadded 
d−1. M5 and M6, characterized by the lowest solids content and sub­
strate load, exhibited the lowest CMY values; nevertheless, Air-NBW 
addition increased CMY in M6 by 17.4%, and M6's specific methane 
rate of 3.9 mL⋅g−1 VSadded d−1 slightly exceeded M5's 3.8 mL⋅g−1 VSadded 
d−1, indicating improved substrate conversion efficiency. The modified 
Gompertz model further indicated improved methane production ki­
netics (Table 2). The experimental data fitted well with the model, with 
R2 values ranging from 0.982 to 0.999. Compared with DW controls, Air- 
NBW increased both the modeled CMY and Rm under all corresponding 
conditions, indicating improved methane production potential and 
conversion kinetics. However, the slightly longer lag phase in Air-NBW 
treatments suggests that enhanced early hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
may have caused transient accumulation of intermediates before stable 
methanogenesis was established.
Overall, Air-NBW-enhanced methane production under all tested 
conditions, but the controlling mechanism differed between thermo­
philic and mesophilic digestion. Under thermophilic conditions, Air- 
NBW promoted rapid hydrolysis and methanogenic conversion, and 
the 1:2 ratio achieved the highest CMY by balancing substrate supply 
and inhibition risk. Under mesophilic conditions, Air-NBW improved

3.2.1. Thermophilic microbial community

Solibacillus, a key hydrolytic genus, secretes extracellular enzymes 
that accelerate polymer breakdown and produces VFAs to sustain 
methanogens [46]; this syntrophic interaction supports overall system 
stability and performance. In Air-NBW treatments, Solibacillus RA 
increased to 41.8% in T2, 29.6% in T4, and 41.8% in T6, compared to 
8.6%, 23.7%, and 25.7% in the corresponding controls (T1, T3, T5). This

philic genus enriched at elevated temperatures, contributes to lactate 
fermentation, polysaccharide degradation, and proteolysis [47]; its 
higher RA in T6 versus T5 aligns with T6's superior substrate conversion 
performance. Corynebacterium efficiently degrades complex organics, 
including cellulose and starch, via diverse extracellular enzymes [48]; 
its RA increased with CM ratio (1:1 > 1:2 > 1:4), explaining elevated 
SCOD in high CM treatments (T1, T2). The coexistence of these hydro­
lytic and fermentative genera suggests that thermophilic digestion 
promoted the rapid conversion of particulate organic matter into soluble 
organics and VFAs. This microbial pattern provides a biological expla­
nation for the early SCOD and VFAs peaks observed under thermophilic 
conditions. By day 60, the bacterial community structure changed 
markedly. The RA of early-stage hydrolytic genera, such as Solibacillus 
and Defluviitalea, decreased substantially to 1.8–11.8% and 0.6–1.0%, 
respectively, while the proportion of unclassified and low-abundance 
taxa increased accordingly. This shift indicates that readily biodegrad­
able substrates were largely depleted during the later-stage of digestion, 
thereby weakening the ecological advantage of hydrolytic and acido­
genic bacteria. This result was consistent with the continuous decline in 
SCOD and VFAs after their early peaks, suggesting that the bacterial 
community gradually shifted from active hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
toward a more substrate-limited state.

3.2.2. Mesophilic microbial community
Bacterial community succession under mesophilic conditions is 
presented in Fig. 8a. At day 3, the bacterial community initially was 
dominated (RA > 3.0%) by Solibacillus (4.1–52.5%), Lysinibacillus 
(7.4–23.2%), 
Acinetobacter 
(1.1–19.5%), 
and 
Corynebacterium 
(0.9–8.5%). Compared with the thermophilic reactors, the mesophilic 
bacterial community maintained higher diversity, which may improve 
ecological resilience but also reflect a slower and less directional func­
tional succession. This pattern was consistent with the delayed SCOD 
peak and prolonged VFAs accumulation observed under mesophilic 
conditions.
Solibacillus plays a key role in hydrolytic breakdown and stabilizes 
AD processes [46]. Its RA in the Air-NBW treatments (M2: 52.5%, M4: 
9.1%) exceeded that in controls (M1: 40.7%, M3: 7.4%), mirroring the 
SCOD trends reported in Section 3.1.2. However, unlike the thermo­
philic system, the strengthened hydrolysis under mesophilic conditions 
did not immediately lead to efficient methane production. Instead, the 
produced soluble substrates and VFAs accumulated during the first 15 
days, indicating that methanogenesis lagged behind hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis. Acinetobacter demonstrates versatile adaptability, thriving 
under both anaerobic and aerobic conditions. This versatility confers 
resilience to environmental fluctuations in AD, thereby supporting 
process stability [49]. Its RA rose with higher Air-NBW dosages (M6: 
19.5% > M4: 2.4% > M2: 1.2%), potentially mitigating microenviron­
mental stress and accelerating recovery from acid inhibition (e.g., 
TVFAs/TA fell below 0.35 by day 25 in M6 versus M5). Corynebacterium, 
a known degrader of complex organics [48], correlated positively with 
valeric acid levels (P < 0.05), indicating that reactors enriched in 
Corynebacterium accumulated more organic acids, consistent with Fig. 3. 
By 60 day, bacterial diversity and dominant taxa declined markedly (e. 
g., Solibacillus to 0.7–21.2%), reflecting endpoint stabilization of SCOD 
and VFAs at low levels. Furthermore, mesophilic digesters exhibited 
higher microbial diversity than thermophilic ones throughout both early 
and late stages, in agreement with Chen et al.

presented in Fig. 8b. At day 3 of mesophilic AD, four genera predomi­
nated (RA > 5%): Methanobrevibacter (43.7–68.7%), Methanosarcina 
(10.1–27.1%), 
Methanothermobacter 
(2.5–6.9%), 
and 
Methanocorpusculum 
(3.6–5.3%).

and 
Meth­

of Methanobrevibacter in mesophilic reactors indicates that hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis was an important pathway for methane 
production under mesophilic conditions. In particular, the RA of Meth­
anobrevibacter was slightly higher in M2 and M6 than in their corre­
sponding DW controls, increasing from 65.0% to 68.7% and from 43.7% 
to 44.9%, respectively. This suggests that Air-NBW may have favored 
the maintenance of hydrogenotrophic methanogens in some mesophilic 
treatments. 
Compared 
with 
acetoclastic 
methanogens, 
hydro­
genotrophic methanogens are generally more tolerant to ammonia 
stress, which may help sustain methanogenic activity in nitrogen-rich 
CM digestion systems [50]. The enrichment of Methanobrevibacter in 
Air-NBW reactors was generally consistent with the improved methane 
yield observed in the corresponding treatments. However, because the 
increase in Methanobrevibacter abundance was not equally evident in all 
Air-NBW groups, the enhanced methane production under mesophilic 
conditions should not be attributed solely to this genus. Rather, it was 
likely associated with the combined effects of improved VFAs turnover, 
alleviated acid inhibition, and the recovery of methanogenic activity 
during the later-stage of digestion. Nevertheless, the overall methane 
production rate under mesophilic conditions remained lower than that 
under thermophilic conditions, indicating that Air-NBW improved 
methanogenic performance but could not completely overcome the ki­
netic limitation imposed by the lower operating temperature. Meth­
anosarcina, which can perform both acetoclastic and hydrogenotrophic 
methanogenesis, was also detected in the mesophilic reactors [51]. 
However, its RA was generally lower than that in the thermophilic 
system, suggesting that the acetoclastic pathway may have been more 
vulnerable to VFAs accumulation and acid stress during mesophilic 
HSAD. This result helps explain why acetate accumulated for a longer 
period under mesophilic conditions, and why methane production was 
delayed despite the continuous release of soluble organic substrates.

indicator of an active methanogenic community.
Therefore, the correlation results support a coordinated mechanism 
for Air-NBW-enhanced thermophilic HSAD. Air-NBW promoted the 
release of soluble organic matter by strengthening the hydrolytic bac­
terial process, while the thermophilic methanogenic community, rep­
resented by Methanosphaera-related methane production correlations, 
facilitated the downstream conversion of intermediates into methane. 
This microbial-process coupling explains why Air-NBW increased SCOD 
peaks without causing persistent instability and ultimately improved 
methane yield and methane production rate. Thus, under thermophilic 
conditions, the enhancement effect of Air-NBW should be understood as 
a coordinated improvement of hydrolysis and methanogenesis rather 
than as the enrichment of a single dominant taxon.

The correlation network between dominant microorganisms and 
environmental/process variables under mesophilic conditions is shown

methane production and the depletion of fermentation intermediates.

did not immediately translate into methane production under meso­

accumulation during the first 15 days, suggesting an imbalance between 
acid production and acid consumption rather than a direct inhibitory 
effect of Solibacillus itself. Corynebacterium was positively correlated 
with valeric acid (P < 0.05), indicating that complex organic matter

For archaeal communities, Methanobrevibacter was positively corre­
lated with TAN (P < 0.05), suggesting that hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogens played an important role in maintaining methanogenic activity 
under nitrogen-rich mesophilic conditions. This is particularly impor­
tant for CM digestion, because protein degradation can continuously 
release ammonium nitrogen. The higher abundance of Methano­
brevibacter in Air-NBW reactors indicates that Air-NBW may have 
improved the tolerance and functional stability of the methanogenic 
community under ammonia and acid stress. Methanobacterium was 
negatively correlated with acetate and propionate (P < 0.05), indicating 
that the increase in this genus was related to the consumption of VFAs or 
their upstream conversion products. This relationship supports the 
performance results showing that Air-NBW accelerated VFAs turnover 
during the later-stage of mesophilic digestion. Propionate is generally 
more difficult to degrade than acetate and is often associated with 
process instability when it accumulates. Therefore, the negative asso­
ciation between Methanobacterium and propionate suggests that hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis may have contributed to relieving acid 
inhibition and restoring digestion stability.
Overall, the correlation network suggests that Air-NBW-enhanced 
mesophilic HSAD through a mechanism different from that under 
thermophilic conditions. Under mesophilic conditions, Air-NBW pro­
moted hydrolysis and acidogenesis, but the lower temperature limited 
the immediate conversion of VFAs to methane, leading to transient acid 
accumulation. Therefore, the subsequent performance improvement 
was mainly associated with accelerated VFAs turnover and the recovery 
of methanogenic activity, particularly hydrogenotrophic methanogens 
such as Methanobrevibacter and Methanobacterium, rather than simply 
with increased soluble organic matter release.
4. Conclusions
In this study, the effects of Air-NBW on the performance and mi­
crobial mechanisms of CM HSAD were investigated under thermophilic 
and mesophilic conditions. The main conclusions are as follows: 
1. Air-NBW-enhanced hydrolysis and acidogenesis during HSAD of CM. 
This was reflected by increased SCOD release and VFAs formation. 
Thermophilic digestion showed faster hydrolysis and VFAs conver­
sion, whereas mesophilic digestion exhibited delayed VFAs con­
sumption and transient acid accumulation.
2. Air-NBW improved process stability by regulating acid accumulation 
and buffering recovery. Although Air-NBW increased early acidifi­
cation pressure in some reactors, TVFAs/TA subsequently declined 
as VFAs were consumed and alkalinity increased. Thermophilic 
systems recovered more rapidly, while mesophilic systems experi­
enced a longer acid-stress period.
3. Air-NBW improved methane production under all tested conditions. 
Compared with the corresponding DW controls, CMY increased by 
10.2–31.9% under thermophilic conditions and by 15.7–21.4% 
under mesophilic conditions. The modified Gompertz model further 
indicated improved methane production kinetics.
4. Microbial and correlation analyses indicated that Air-NBW-enhanced 
HSAD through coordinated hydrolysis and methanogenesis. Ther­
mophilic enhancement was associated with efficient organic solu­
bilization 
and 
methanogenic 
conversion, 
while 
mesophilic 
enhancement relied more on VFAs turnover and methanogenic 
recovery.
